name: AI Litigation
blurb: Living case pages for AI lawsuits in United States courts, refreshed from the dockets daily.

reading.body:
The AI litigation hub contains no case entries itself but points to two resources: a daily-refreshed tracker of current lawsuits by claim family, and profiles of older precedents AI defendants rely on.

The tracker labels every case across eleven claim families, from copyright and right of publicity to product liability, hiring discrimination, biometric privacy, securities fraud, trade secrets, platform access, patent, consumer protection, and government contracts. The precedents resource covers a small set of older decisions, including Sony, Campbell, Google Books, Van Buren, hiQ, and Zeran, each with what it held, why AI defendants cite it, and where the analogy is weakest. Together they show that current AI litigation is argued through a narrow set of pre-generative precedents, while the tracker refreshes daily.

This data says nothing about compute, data centers, or grid capacity. It covers only United States courts and does not report outcomes, settlements, or case volumes beyond the linked resources.

children.name: AI Lawsuit Tracker

children.desc: The older decisions AI defendants are actually relying on. Every current AI copyright, scraping and defamation case is argued out of a small set of precedents decided long before generative models existed: Sony on substantial non-infringing use, Campbell and Google Books on transformative purpose, Van Buren and hiQ on scraping, Zeran on Section 230. Each profile states what the case held, why AI defendants cite it, and where the analogy is weakest, with a link to the opinion itself.
children.name: AI Case Law: The Precedents Behind the Defenses
